title: Are 324 and 156 perfect squares? What do their primes say?
description: Three hundred twenty four and one hundred fifty six are each broken into primes, and the primes are shared into two equal groups. One number shares out evenly and the other leaves primes alone. Keeko doubts the second number, because it has one pair of twos.
teaching_notes: One idea: a perfect square's primes split into two equal groups, so every prime comes in a pair. Watch for students who see one pair and stop checking the other primes.

source: Use prime factorisation to decide whether 324 and 156 are pe
video_script.why: The child uses prime factorisation to test a perfect square by sharing the primes into two equal groups.
video_script.substitution: Write the number as a string of primes and try to share them into two equal groups.
video_script.anchor: the two numbers of the book question, three hundred twenty four and one hundred fifty six, written on cards
video_script.wrong_answer: one hundred fifty six is a perfect square
video_script.wrong_move: Keeko sees one pair of twos in one hundred fifty six and says it is a perfect square. The three and the thirteen have no partners, so it is not.
video_script.payoff_line: Three hundred twenty four is eighteen squared, a perfect square

final_answer.value: 324 is a perfect square with √324 = 18; 156 is not a perfect square
final_answer.spoken: three hundred twenty four is eighteen squared, a perfect square; one hundred fifty six is not a perfect square

maths_rules: 156 = 2 × 2 × 3 × 13; the 3 and the 13 appear once each, so 156 is not a perfect square
video_script.design: One idea: two equal groups of primes. Wrong idea: one pair is enough. The two number cards stay in the anchor band and the prime boards sit on the working board.

narration: <bookmark mark='sq'/>A perfect square is a whole number multiplied by itself.
<bookmark mark='groups'/>That means its prime factors must share into two equal groups, one for each copy.
<bookmark mark='pf'/>Prime factorisation means writing a number as primes multiplied together.
<bookmark mark='given'/>Given, the numbers are three hundred twenty four and one hundred fifty six.

<bookmark mark='list1'/>It is two times two times three times three times three times three.

narration: <bookmark mark='share'/>Step two, share these primes into two equal groups.
<bookmark mark='why'/>A square is a number times itself, so each group is one copy.
<bookmark mark='each'/>Each group gets one two and two threes.

beats.on_screen: Answer: 2 × 3 × 3 = 18, so 324 = 18 × 18 = 18², a perfect square; 156 is not a perfect square

narration: <bookmark mark='ans'/>Each group is two times three times three, which is eighteen.
Eighteen times eighteen is three hundred twenty four.
<bookmark mark='sq'/>Three hundred twenty four is eighteen squared, a perfect square.
<bookmark mark='no'/>One hundred fifty six is not a perfect square.
<bookmark mark='hand'/>Keeko has raised a hand. Let us check the doubt and solve it.

narration: <bookmark mark='doubt'/>Keeko thinks one hundred fifty six is a perfect square, because it has a pair of twos.
<bookmark mark='alone'/>But look at the three and the thirteen. Each one appears only once.
<bookmark mark='fix'/>Every prime needs a partner, not only the twos.
